paras: The attempted lynching of Robert Gibson took place at Barnesville, Belmont County, Ohio, on the night of May 24, 1888, when a crowd broke into the town lockup, seized Gibson, a Black man accused of sexually assaulting a five-year-old white girl, and whipped him in a field outside town. After proposals to hang him were voted down, he was returned to the officers alive, although the first wire report said he had been hanged. The case drew further notice when the county grand jury declined to indict Gibson and Barnesville men, including the girl's father, were indicted for the mob's work.

On Thursday, May 24, employees of the First National Bank in Barnesville saw Gibson with the young daughter of Frank Jeffries behind the bank building and reported him. The papers stated the charge in different terms, from rape to "indecent assault" to attempted rape. The father swore out a warrant, and Gibson was arrested a short distance east of town, by deputy W. H. Brown according to the Belmont Chronicle, and placed in the lockup.

Shortly after 11 p.m., Jeffries called out, "Gentlemen, here I am, who will protect me?" and, in the Intelligencer's account, about a hundred men answered and rushed through the mayor's office into the jail yard. The Belmont Chronicle put the crowd at "possibly fifty or a hundred men," led by a half-dozen well-known "negro haters," and said they struck while Marshal Renner was out getting a lunch. They overpowered Constable Bulger and battered down the barred door with sledges; Renner returned and used his mace but was himself overpowered and "roughly used."

Gibson was hustled to a lot just outside town while the crowd shouted "hang him" and "cut his throat." According to the wire account, a vote to hang him failed, a proposal to emasculate him also failed, and a flogging was chosen. He was stripped, tied to a tree and whipped with beech switches, then taken back and delivered to Marshal Renner. His back and head were cut and bruised, though the Wheeling Register called the injuries "painful but not serious."

On May 25 Gibson waived examination before Justice Baker and was sent to the county jail at St. Clairsville. That afternoon his brother, Minor Gibson, was arrested on charges of exposing himself to women, and the Register's correspondent wrote that only the quick removal of both men prevented "a double lynching." The grand jury, reporting on May 29, ignored the case against Robert Gibson and returned five indictments against his brother for indecent exposure. The court then ordered Robert Gibson discharged from custody, while Minor Gibson pleaded not guilty and was held for trial.

A Bellaire dispatch of June 14 named six indicted men: Francis Jeffries, the girl's father, W. H. Brown, Jonathan Ellis, Sol Morris, Asa Browers and Frank Moore. They pleaded not guilty and gave $200 bond each; the same dispatch reported Gibson working in Bellaire. No report of a trial of the indicted men or of Minor Gibson appears in the coverage.

The earliest wire report, printed by the Indianapolis Journal on May 25 under "Lynched for a Monstrous Crime," said the mob had hanged Gibson to a tree. The next day the Wheeling Intelligencer headed its special dispatch "A HANGING BEE SPOILED" and called Gibson "the Barnesville Fiend." Other papers used headlines such as "RAPIST GIBSON," "A BRUTE FLOGGED" and "A RAPIST FLOGGED," stating the accusation as fact.

The Register's correspondent wrote that the mob's work was approved "so far as it went" but faulted as not severe enough, and the Maysville Evening Bulletin headlined "Indignant Citizens Declare It Too Lenient." The Belmont Chronicle at the county seat took a different line, calling Gibson's conduct "bestial" but holding that the mob's defiance of law "cannot be tolerated."

Short wire versions ran in the Memphis Appeal, Kentucky weeklies and Michigan's Diamond Drill. Ohio state-news columns repeated flatly that Gibson had "outraged a little white girl." The True Northerner of Paw Paw, Michigan, alone reported that investigation had "proved the colored man innocent."
The True Northerner said thirty prominent citizens were indicted, while the Bellaire dispatch named six "of the Barnesville parties indicted," leaving the full number unclear.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Robert Gibson
bases: A crowd broke Gibson out of the Barnesville lockup intending, by several accounts, to hang him, voted on hanging, and whipped him instead (A3, A6, A17).

A crowd of fifty to a hundred took Gibson from custody to punish an alleged assault (A3, A11), but he was whipped and returned alive (A5, A6, A19); only the first wire report (A1) said he was hanged, and later reports contradict it.

Independent local and regional dispatches (A3, A5, A6, A11) and court records (A12, A19) agree on the seizure, whipping and survival; the lone hanging report (A1) is an early error contradicted by all later coverage.

framing.detail: Indianapolis Journal: 'Lynched for a Monstrous Crime', reporting the hanging as fact.
Wheeling Intelligencer: 'A HANGING BEE SPOILED... The Barnesville Fiend', 'A Very Indignant Mob'; accusation as fact, mob's 'judge' in quotes.
Wheeling Register: 'RAPIST GIBSON... The Colored Wretch'; the mob's work approved but 'not being severe enough', and promptness of authorities 'spoiled a good item'.
Maysville Evening Bulletin: 'A RAPIST FLOGGED', 'Indignant Citizens Declare It Too Lenient'.
Springfield Daily Republic: 'A BRUTE FLOGGED'; Memphis Appeal: 'A Negro Lashed in Ohio'.
Belmont Chronicle: calls Gibson's act 'bestial' but says the mob's defiance of law 'cannot be tolerated'.
True Northerner: 'Indicted for Attempting a Lynching'; says Gibson was proved innocent.

The grand jury ignored the case (A12, A13); the Belmont Chronicle says it found no evidence on which to indict (A11).
A20 says 'Six of the Barnesville parties indicted', which may mean six of a larger number.
Minor; both put it just outside town.
